title: A school for beginners (Prologue)
hook: Benedict hopes to set down nothing harsh or burdensome

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rule: Benedict's book for monks opens with one word, listen. Your line was the ear of the heart. Who did you listen to all the way to the end? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

A bright sticker on the back of a car: student driver. The cars behind it tend to soften. They give more room. They don't honk when it stalls at the light. The sticker doesn't make the driver any better. It just tells the truth: this person is learning, so be patient. Saint Benedict, near the end of the Prologue to his Rule, puts something like that sticker on the whole monastery. Today: a school for beginners.
screen: `STUDENT DRIVER.` → `THE CARS BEHIND GIVE ROOM.` → `BENEDICT'S STICKER.`

segments.voice: Benedict tells his monks what he's building. In Latin: dominici schola servitii, a school of the Lord's service. Not a fortress for the already holy. A school. A place where people come because they don't know yet. Then comes the hope that gives this day its line. Benedict says that in setting it up, he hopes to lay down nothing harsh, nothing heavy. He's honest, though. He admits some things may feel a little strict, for good reasons: to correct faults, to protect love. And he asks the beginner not to run away in fear when that happens, because the way in is narrow at the start. Then he makes a promise. As someone goes on in this life and in faith, the heart grows wider, and they run the way of God's commandments with a sweetness of love that's hard to put into words. That's the Rule borrowing a line from the Psalms. In the Douay-Rheims: "I have run the way of thy commandments, when thou didst enlarge my heart." Look at the shape of it. Narrow at the start, wider as you go. Strict in places, but never meant to crush. Benedict isn't writing for heroes. He's writing for people who will stall at the light. And at the very end of the Rule, he'll call it a little rule for beginners. Not just the first chapter. The whole book. In Benedict's school, nobody graduates.
screen: `A SCHOOL OF THE LORD'S SERVICE.` · `NOTHING HARSH, NOTHING HEAVY.` · `NARROW AT THE START.` · `THE HEART GROWS WIDER.` · then, large: `WHEN THOU DIDST ENLARGE MY HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go easy on yourself as a beginner. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you're new at, or keep starting over. Prayer, maybe. A language, a diet, a new job, being a parent. Notice the voice in your head that talks to you about it. Is it harsh? Now try Benedict's tone instead. Strict where it matters, nothing harsh, nothing heavy. Say to yourself, quietly: I'm learning. If you pray, you can ask God to widen your heart a little at a time. The bell holds the time.

A school for beginners. Benedict's picture of the monastery: a school of the Lord's service, where he hopes to set down nothing harsh or heavy, and where the heart grows wider as you go. Today's word.
Your line: nothing harsh. Today, when you stall at something new, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a student driver. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Benedictine communities welcome newcomers through a period of trial and learning, and Benedictines describe their whole life as a school of the Lord's service.

notes: The Prologue's closing section is paraphrased, not quoted (Gasquet 1909 wording unverified). Latin to confirm: 'Constituenda est ergo nobis dominici schola servitii... nihil asperum, nihil grave nos constituturos speramus'.
'The way in is narrow at the start' paraphrases the Prologue's 'via salutis, quae nisi angusto initio incipienda'; confirm.
Ch. 73's 'little rule for beginners' is referred to ahead of day 1204, which teaches it; editor may prefer to trim.
howItsDone's 'period of trial' refers to the postulancy/novitiate (ch. 58); confirm.
